title.text:
Binary classification (yes or
no) and how to measure it

objects.text: Can a binary classifier say yes or no to "high cooling load", and how do we count its true and false positives and negatives?

CML3112  |  Civil Engineering and Architecture  |  Week 9, class 2 of 4  |  Tuesday 10 November 2026, 11:00 to 14:00
KLAi  |  International University of East Africa  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Class 2. Last week the model gave you a number. Today it answers yes or no, which is called binary classification. We stay with the building data, and the question is whether the cooling load reaches its limit. You will see how a classifier is built, and the most important lesson of the day: how to count its mistakes. The ideas come first, then the lab, then a short quiz.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Turn the cooling load into a binary label (positive class or negative class) with a limit
Train logistic regression and a decision tree classifier, and work out a confusion matrix and four scores by hand
Move the decision threshold and explain precision, recall, F1, the ROC curve and AUC in plain words, with the formulas

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can turn the cooling load into a binary label, positive or negative, using a limit. You can train two classifiers, and work out their confusion matrix and four scores by hand. And you can move the decision threshold and explain precision, recall, F1, the ROC curve and AUC in plain words, and write the formulas.

Today ends with a short quiz of five questions that covers Class 1 and Class 2. It opens in the last 20 minutes of the class and stays open for 24 hours, and the lab becomes part B of the first assignment.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is a baseline model for?
2.  What does the unit of the MAE tell you?
3.  Why do we split the rows by equipment group?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Class 1. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is a baseline model for? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A baseline model is the simplest possible prediction, here the mean of the training target. Every model must beat it. If a model cannot, it has learned nothing useful.

Question two. What does the unit of the MAE tell you? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The mean absolute error (MAE) is in the unit of the target variable, so an MAE of 2 kW means the prediction error is about 2 kW on average.

Question three. Why do we split the rows by equipment group? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. So that the validation set holds whole building groups the model has never met, which is the situation in real use.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Class 1

rows.text: What is a baseline model for?
A baseline model is the simplest possible prediction, here the mean of the training target. Every model must beat it. If a model cannot, it has learned nothing useful.
What does the unit of the MAE tell you?
The mean absolute error (MAE) is in the unit of the target variable, so an MAE of 2 kW means the prediction error is about 2 kW on average.
Why do we split the rows by equipment group?
So that the validation set holds whole building groups the model has never met, which is the situation in real use.

objects.text: Check your own answer against these before we start today.

slides.notes:
Here are the short answers to the three questions, so you can check yourself and keep them for revision. A baseline model is the simplest possible prediction, and every model must beat it. The unit of the MAE is the unit of the target variable, so it tells you the typical size of the prediction error in plain words.

And we split by equipment group so that the validation set holds whole building groups the model has never seen. Did your own answer include the reason in each case?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Two possible answers: the positive class (yes, such as "overheating") and the negative class (no). The label is 1 or 0.
The cut-off on the predicted probability. At or above it the model predicts positive (yes).
A table of actual against predicted classes: TP, FN, FP and TN (true or false, positive or negative).
Precision: of the predicted positives, the share that are right. Recall (sensitivity): of the actual positives, the share found.
The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate. AUC, the area under it, is 0 to 1: how well positives rank above negatives.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Binary classification. Two possible answers: the positive class (yes, such as "overheating") and the negative class (no). The label is 1 or 0.

Decision threshold. The cut-off on the predicted probability. At or above it the model predicts positive (yes).

Confusion matrix. A table of actual against predicted classes: TP, FN, FP and TN (true or false, positive or negative).

Precision and recall. Precision: of the predicted positives, the share that are right. Recall (sensitivity): of the actual positives, the share found.

ROC curve and AUC. The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate. AUC, the area under it, is 0 to 1: how well positives rank above negatives.

title.text:
Binary classification gives a yes or no answer
that tells a plant operator whether to act

objects.alt: Binary classification gives a yes or no answer that tells a plant operator whether to act

objects.text: Binary classification has two classes: yes (positive) and no (negative). The question: is it high cooling load?

runs.text: In Class 1 (regression) the model gave a number, such as the cooling load in kW.
Today the model reads the features and gives one of two classes: yes or no.

slides.notes:
Last week the model gave you a number, for example the cooling load in kW. A number is useful, but in practice someone has to decide whether to act. So today the question is a yes or no question, which is called binary classification: is it high cooling load?

Yes is the positive class and no is the negative class. A reading arrives, the model says yes or no, and a person acts. For the building data the example is: yes: start extra cooling early. That is an illustration, and your own plant may do something different.

What decision would you attach to a yes in your own field?

title.text:
Regression predicts a number
and classification predicts a class

objects.text: Regression

runs.text: The answer is a number in kW
Class 1: linear regression and a tree
Scored by prediction error: MAE and RMSE

objects.text: Classification

runs.text: The answer is a class: positive or negative
Today: logistic regression and a decision tree classifier
Scored by counting TP, FN, FP and TN

objects.text: Same data and same split as Class 1. Only the question changes.

slides.notes:
Here is the difference in one slide. In regression the answer is a number, and we measure the size of the prediction error with MAE and RMSE. In classification the answer is a class, here positive or negative, and the error is a different thing: the answer is either right or wrong, so we count.

The data are the same, the split is the same, and the equipment groups are the same. Only the question changes. That is why the measures change too, and most of today is about those new measures.

title.text:
A limit on the cooling load turns each
row into a positive or negative label

objects.alt: A limit on the cooling load turns each row into a positive or negative label

objects.text: The label (target variable) is positive (1, yes) when the cooling load is 54 kW or more, and negative (0, no) below.

runs.text: Each dot is one row of the training set. Gold dots are positive: 19 of 58.
Validation set: 3 of 15 rows are positive.
The features are still load_pct and ambient_c.

slides.notes:
Here are the training rows again, with load on the bottom and the cooling load up the side. The dashed line is the limit, 54 kW. A row at or above the line gets the label positive, which is yes, and a row below it gets the label negative, which is no.

That rule makes the label. In the training set 19 of 58 rows are positive, and in the validation set 3 of 15 are positive. The model still sees only load and ambient temperature as features. The label is the answer it must learn to give. Which dots would you worry about most?

title.text:
The majority-class baseline always answers no, is right
on 80 percent of rows and finds no actual positive

objects.alt: The majority-class baseline always answers no, is right on 80 percent of rows and finds no actual positive

objects.text: The majority-class baseline always predicts the more common class, here no. Accuracy is the share of rows answered correctly.

runs.text: Always no is right on 12 of 15 validation rows: accuracy 0.80.
It finds none of the 3 actual positive rows.
A model must beat accuracy 0.80 and also find positive rows.

slides.notes:
Look at the validation set. 12 of the 15 rows are no, and 3 are yes. A model that says no every time is right on 12 of 15 rows, an accuracy of 0.80. That sounds good, yet it finds none of the 3 actual positive cases, and those are the ones we care about.

This is called the majority-class baseline, because it always predicts the most common class. It is the simplest model, and every real model must beat it. The data are imbalanced, which means one class is much rarer than the other, so accuracy cannot be the only measure we use today.

title.text:
Standardisation (StandardScaler) puts load_pct and
ambient_c on the same scale before the model learns

objects.alt: Standardisation (StandardScaler) puts load_pct and ambient_c on the same scale before the model learns

objects.text: Standardisation rewrites each feature as a z-score.

runs.text: A z-score counts how many standard deviations (the typical distance from the mean) a value lies above or below the training mean.
Each table row is one training row (training row 1 (record_id 1) is first).

slides.notes:
The two features live on different scales. Load runs from about 21 to 93, and ambient temperature from about 18 to 34. Standardisation rewrites each feature as a z-score, which is how many standard deviations it sits above or below its training mean. The scikit-learn tool is called StandardScaler.

Take training row 1: load 59.15 minus the mean 59.89, divided by the standard deviation 22.73, gives -0.03. The mean and the standard deviation are learned from the training set only, exactly like the median imputation in Class 1. Why must the validation set not help decide them?

title.text:
The z-score formula: subtract the training mean,
then divide by the training standard deviation

objects.alt: The z-score formula: subtract the training mean, then divide by the training standard deviation

rows.text: The standardised value (z-score): 0 is the mean, 1 is one standard deviation above
The training mean of that column
The training standard deviation of that column

objects.text: Subscript 1 is load_pct and 2 is ambient_c. Validation rows are standardised with the same mu and sigma.

slides.notes:
Here is standardisation in the usual notation. A raw value x, minus the training mean mu, divided by the training standard deviation sigma, gives the z-score x prime. For load, mu is 59.89 percent and sigma is 22.73. For ambient temperature, mu is 26.33 degrees and sigma is 4.55.

Training row 1 gives -0.03 for load and 1.18 for ambient temperature. The small numbers 1 and 2 only say which feature we mean. Check the load line with your calculator before we go on.

title.text:
Logistic regression passes a linear score through the
sigmoid (logistic) function, which stays between 0 and 1

objects.alt: Logistic regression passes a linear score through the sigmoid (logistic) function, which stays between 0 and 1

objects.text: The sigmoid (logistic) function turns any score into a probability from 0 to 1.

runs.text: A probability of 0.5 means the two classes are equally likely.
The decision threshold is a cut-off on the probability: at or above it the model predicts positive (yes), below it negative (no).

slides.notes:
Why not use a straight line to predict yes or no?

Because a linear function keeps going, below zero and above one, and a probability cannot. Logistic regression first builds a score from the features, in the same way as the linear regression in Class 1. Then it passes the score through an S-shaped curve called the sigmoid, or logistic function.

Very low scores become a probability near 0, very high scores near 1, and a score of 0 becomes exactly 0.5. The gold dot is one real row, and we work it out by hand in a moment. Then a decision threshold turns the probability into a prediction.

title.text:
Logistic regression in three lines:
score, probability, prediction

objects.alt: Logistic regression in three lines: score, probability, prediction

rows.text: Weights (coefficients): rise in z per standard deviation

slides.notes:
This is the whole of logistic regression in three lines. First the score z: an intercept b zero, plus a weight times each standardised feature. Our learned numbers are an intercept of -1.71, a weight of 2.79 for load and a weight of 0.73 for ambient temperature. Second, the sigmoid function turns the score into a probability p between 0 and 1.

Third, the prediction: the class is positive when p is at or above the decision threshold t, and negative otherwise. Both weights are positive, so more load or more heat pushes the score toward yes.

title.text:
Worked example: validation row 3
gets p = 0.45, so the model predicts no

objects.alt: Worked example: validation row 3 gets p = 0.45, so the model predicts no

objects.text: Validation row 3 (record_id 17): load_pct 61.76 %, ambient_c 34.28 deg C. Actual class: positive.

runs.text: p = 0.45 is below the threshold 0.5, so the prediction is no: a false negative (FN).
One standard deviation more load_pct adds 2.79 to z. One more of ambient_c adds 0.73.

slides.notes:
This is validation row 3, which is record_id 17 in the file. After standardisation, its load is 0.08 and its ambient temperature 1.75. Multiply each by its weight, add the intercept of -1.71, and the score is -0.20. The sigmoid turns that into a probability of 0.45. At the usual decision threshold of 0.5 the model predicts no, and the actual class was positive, so this row is a false negative (FN).

Because the features are standardised, one standard deviation more load adds 2.79 to the score and one more of temperature adds 0.73. The products may differ in the last digit because of rounding.

title.text:
A decision tree classifier can also answer yes
or no, and it does not need standardisation

objects.alt: A decision tree classifier can also answer yes or no, and it does not need standardisation

objects.text: A row follows the answers down the tree until it reaches one leaf node, a yellow box.

runs.text: Each question is an internal node: a split on a feature.
A leaf node predicts yes when most training rows that ended there are yes.
Validation accuracy: 0.87.

slides.notes:
The second model is a decision tree classifier, the same idea as Class 1 with one change at the bottom. In Class 1 each leaf node predicted an average. Now each leaf node gives the majority class of the training rows that ended there: yes if most of them are yes, otherwise no.

A row starts at the top, follows the answers to each question, and stops at one leaf node, the yellow box. On the validation set this tree reaches an accuracy of 0.87, but accuracy is not the whole story, so we count the mistakes next. Which question comes first?

title.text: How to read the tree

objects.text: A leaf node (a yellow box) predicts the majority class of the training rows that ended there.
max_depth is a hyperparameter, a setting chosen before training. It is the largest number of questions (internal nodes) a row can be asked on the way down. Here it is 3.
A deeper tree can fit the training set so closely that it overfits: it fits the noise. Class 3 tests that.
The questions use the real feature values, so a tree needs no standardisation.

slides.notes:
Four things to notice about the tree. A leaf node, the yellow box, gives the majority class of the training rows that ended there. The hyperparameter max_depth is the largest number of questions a row can be asked on the way down, and here it is three. A deeper tree asks more questions and can fit the training set more closely, even to the point of overfitting, and Class 3 tests that.

Finally, the questions use the real load and temperature, so a tree needs no standardisation. Why would a tree not care about the units of load?

title.text:
The confusion matrix counts true
and false positives and negatives

objects.alt: The confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives

objects.text: Logistic regression, decision threshold 0.5, validation set. Positive class: high cooling load.

runs.text: Each of the 15 rows lands in exactly one box.
Rows: Actual class. Columns: Predicted class, as in scikit-learn.
FP is a false warning. FN is a missed case.

slides.notes:
Here is the logistic regression on the 15 validation rows at decision threshold 0.5. Each row falls into one of four boxes. There are 2 true positives, TP: the model said yes and it was yes. There are 1 false negatives, FN: the model said no, but it was yes.

There are 0 false positives, FP: the model said yes, but it was no. And there are 12 true negatives, TN: the model said no and it was no. The four counts add to 15. Rows are the Actual class and columns are the Predicted class, the same layout scikit-learn prints. Everything else today is arithmetic on these four numbers.

title.text:
Accuracy and precision are worked out
from the four counts TP, FP, FN and TN

objects.alt: Accuracy and precision are worked out from the four counts TP, FP, FN and TN

rows.text: True positive: predicted positive, actually positive
False positive: predicted positive, actually negative
False negative: predicted negative, actually positive
True negative: predicted negative, actually negative
All rows scored: TP + TN + FP + FN

objects.text: Counts are for logistic regression at decision threshold 0.5.

slides.notes:
Now the formulas, with the standard names. TP, FP, FN and TN are the four counts of the confusion matrix. Accuracy is the right answers, TP plus TN, over all n rows: 2 plus 12, over 15, is 0.93. Precision looks only at the rows where the model predicted positive: TP over TP plus FP, which is 2 over 2, or 1.00.

Compare the accuracy with the majority-class baseline of 0.80. Which of the four counts does precision ignore?

title.text:
Recall (sensitivity) and F1: how many actual
positives we find, and one blended score

objects.alt: Recall (sensitivity) and F1: how many actual positives we find, and one blended score

rows.text: Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate): share of actual positives found
Precision: the share of the model's positive predictions that are right
The F1 score, a blend of P and R. It is low when either one is low
True positives and false negatives (previous slide)

objects.text: Same F1 from the counts: 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) = 4 / (4 + 0 + 1) = 0.80.

slides.notes:
Recall asks: of all the rows that are actually positive, how many did we find?

That is TP over TP plus FN, which is 2 over 3, or 0.67. Recall is also called sensitivity. F1 blends precision P and recall R into one number, two P R over P plus R. With P of 1.00 and R of 0.67 we get 0.80. The note shows a second way to write it straight from the counts, and it gives the same 0.80.

F1 is low if either precision or recall is low, so you cannot hide a weak one. Which score would you protect if a false negative is dangerous?

title.text:
The four scores in words: the
question each one answers

rows.text: Out of all rows, how often is the prediction right?
Of the rows the model predicted positive, how many are really positive?
Of the rows that are really positive, how many did the model find?
One number that blends precision and recall

objects.text: Counts: TP 2, FN 1, FP 0, TN 12. The majority-class baseline has accuracy 0.80.

slides.notes:
Here are the same four scores in plain words, next to the arithmetic you have just seen. Accuracy: how often the prediction is right. Precision: when the model predicts positive, how often it is right. Recall, or sensitivity: of the actual positive cases, how many it found. F1: one number that blends the last two.

With your counts they are 0.93, 1.00, 0.67 and 0.80. Notice that accuracy sits above the majority-class baseline of 0.80, but only by a small margin. Please check one line on paper with me before we move on.

title.text:
A false negative and a false positive
cost different things for a building

objects.text: False negative (FN)

runs.text: Predicted no, but actually yes.
The cooling plant is not ready.
Rooms can get too warm.
Every FN lowers recall.

objects.text: False positive (FP)

runs.text: Predicted yes, but actually no.
Extra cooling starts early for nothing.
It wastes some energy.
Every FP lowers precision.

objects.text: Here a false negative costs more, so we watch recall.

slides.notes:
The two mistakes are not equal. A false negative means the model said no, and the cooling load did reach its limit. The cooling plant is not ready. Rooms can get too warm. A false positive means the model said yes and nothing happened. Extra cooling starts early for nothing.

It wastes some energy. These descriptions are my illustration, and your own site may weigh them differently. The point is that you decide which mistake hurts more before you choose a decision threshold. If false negatives hurt more, you care most about recall. If false positives hurt more, you care most about precision.

Which would you protect in your own field?

title.text:
Logistic regression and the decision tree
give different counts on the same 15 rows

objects.text: Logistic regression has the higher F1 here (0.80 against 0.67). With 15 rows, read the gap as a hint. Precision of 0.00 for the majority-class baseline means 0 of 0: it never predicts positive.

slides.notes:
Here are the two models side by side on the same 15 validation rows, with the majority-class baseline for comparison. Logistic regression has 2 true positives and 1 false negatives, with 0 false positives. The tree has 2 true positives and 1 false negatives, with 1 false positives.

The baseline has an accuracy of 0.80 but finds nothing, so its precision and recall are zero. Logistic regression has the higher F1 here (0.80 against 0.67). With 15 rows, read the gap as a hint. Remember that one row changes these numbers a lot when there are only 15 rows.

title.text:
Moving the decision threshold changes the precision-recall
trade-off: more positives found, more false positives

objects.alt: Moving the decision threshold changes the precision-recall trade-off: more positives found, more false positives

objects.text: A lower decision threshold raises recall but gives more false positives. This is the precision-recall trade-off.

runs.text: Each dot is one validation row. Gold: actual positive. White: actual negative.
Validation row 3 (record_id 17) is an actual positive with p = 0.45: predicted positive at 0.3, negative at 0.5 and 0.7.

slides.notes:
Each dot is one validation row, placed by the probability the model gave it. Gold dots are actual positives and white dots are actual negatives. The dashed lines are three decision thresholds. A row at or above the line is predicted positive. Validation row 3 is an actual positive.

Its probability is 0.45, so the model predicts positive at decision threshold 0.3, and negative at 0.5 and 0.7. Below the picture you can read TP, FN and FP for each threshold. Sliding the line left finds more positives, and sliding it right gives fewer false positives. That is the precision-recall trade-off.

Where would you put it for your own site?

title.text:
Each decision threshold gives its
own counts and its own scores

objects.text: TP: true positives. FN: false negatives. FP: false positives. At 0.7 no row is predicted positive, so precision shows 0.00. 0.5 to 0.3: recall goes from 0.67 to 1.00; FP goes from 0 to 1.

slides.notes:
These are the three decision thresholds as numbers. Lowering the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3: recall goes from 0.67 to 1.00, and false positives (FP) goes from 0 to 1. Raising it from 0.5 to 0.7: recall goes from 0.67 to 0.00, and false positives (FP) stays at 0.

At 0.7 the model predicts positive for no row at all, so precision has nothing to divide and we show it as 0.00. A lower threshold usually raises recall, and a higher one does the opposite. So there is no single best threshold, only a best one for the cost of the mistakes at your site.

title.text:
On a larger set, a lower decision threshold finds
more positives and also gives more false positives

objects.text: Illustrative example (hypothetical data), not from our data. TPR is the same as recall. Each row of this table becomes one point on a ROC curve.

slides.notes:
This table uses illustrative numbers, made up to show an idea that our 15 rows cannot show for every cohort. Imagine a larger set with 10 actual positive rows and 90 actual negative rows. At a low decision threshold of 0.2 the model finds all 10, but it also gives 27 false positives.

At a high threshold of 0.8 it gives only 1 false positive, but it finds just 4 of the 10. The two right-hand columns are the true positive rate, the share of actual positives found, which is recall, and the false positive rate, the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged positive.

Each row becomes one point on the ROC curve in a moment. Which row would you choose if a false negative is dangerous?

title.text:
Two rates give the points of the ROC curve: the false
positive rate (FPR) and the true positive rate (TPR)

objects.alt: Two rates give the points of the ROC curve: the false positive rate (FPR) and the true positive rate (TPR)

rows.text: False positive rate: share of actual negatives (FP + TN) predicted positive
True positive rate: share of actual positives (TP + FN) found. Same as recall
True negative rate: TN / (TN + FP). Equals 1 - FPR

slides.notes:
The ROC curve needs two rates. The false positive rate, FPR, is FP over FP plus TN: of all the rows that are actually negative, what share did we wrongly flag as positive. At decision threshold 0.5 that is 0 over 12, or 0.00. The true positive rate, TPR, is the same thing as recall, also called sensitivity: 2 over 3, or 0.67.

Specificity is the share of actual negatives we clear correctly, which is one minus FPR. Each threshold gives one pair of rates, and each pair is one point on the ROC graph that follows. Why is a low FPR good, and a high TPR good?

title.text:
The ROC curve plots one point for every
decision threshold: FPR across, TPR up

objects.alt: The ROC curve plots one point for every decision threshold: FPR across, TPR up

objects.text: ROC is short for receiver operating characteristic. It is a graph with one point per decision threshold.

runs.text: Each black dot is one threshold. 15 validation rows give only 16 points, so the line is a staircase.
The three red dots are our thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 from the table. The gold area under the line is the AUC.

slides.notes:
The ROC curve is a graph, and ROC stands for receiver operating characteristic. For every decision threshold we work out two rates and plot one point: the false positive rate across, and the true positive rate up. The black dots are every threshold that changes a prediction on our rows.

We have only 15 rows, so there are only 16 points, and the line climbs in steps like a staircase. The three red dots are the thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 from the table. A curve that hugs the top left corner is good, because it finds many positives with few false positives.

The dashed line is random guessing. The area under the line is the AUC, here 1.00. Why does our curve have so few points?

title.text:
AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and
on a large dataset the curve is smooth

objects.alt: AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and on a large dataset the curve is smooth

objects.text: AUC (area under the curve) is the chance that an actual positive row scores higher than an actual negative row.

runs.text: Ours: 36 pairs (3 x 12), and 36 of 36 pairs are in the right order: AUC 1.00.
The curve is illustrative. With thousands of rows it looks smooth. AUC 0.5 is random guessing.

slides.notes:
Here is what the AUC means in words. Take one actual positive row and one actual negative row. AUC is the chance that the model gives the positive row the higher probability. We have 3 positive rows and 12 negative rows, so 36 pairs, and 36 of them are in the right order.

That gives 1.00. A perfect score on 15 rows is a warm hint, and it promises nothing about new equipment. The curve in the picture is illustrative. On a large dataset there are thousands of thresholds, the dots sit almost on top of each other, and the staircase becomes a smooth curve.

An AUC of 0.5 is a coin flip, and 1.0 is perfect. Why is this score independent of any single decision threshold?

title.text:
With 15 rows and 3 actual
positives, every score here is shaky

objects.text: The validation set has 15 rows and only 3 actual positive rows.
If one prediction changed, recall would move by 0.33 and accuracy by 0.07.
These numbers teach you how the scores work. They are too few to prove which model is better.
Class 3 shows how to test a model with more care.

slides.notes:
I want to be careful about the limits. The validation set has only 15 rows and 3 of them are actual positives. If the model got one more positive right, the recall would move by 0.33. If it got one more row right, the accuracy would move by 0.07.

So the numbers on these slides are good for learning the scores, and weak as proof that one model beats another. Next class we look at tests that use more rows and give us more reason to trust a number. Keep that caution in mind in the lab.

title.text:
Summary: judge a binary classifier
by counting each kind of mistake

objects.text: Make a label from the target with a limit: positive class or negative class.
Standardise the features. Logistic regression turns a score into a probability with the sigmoid function.
A decision threshold turns the probability into a predicted class.
Count TP, FP, FN and TN, then work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
Move the decision threshold, or read the ROC curve and AUC, to balance recall against precision.

slides.notes:
Here is the whole class in five lines. Make a label from the target with a limit. Standardise the features, and let logistic regression turn a score into a probability. Use a decision threshold to turn the probability into a predicted class. Count the answers in a confusion matrix, and work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1.

Then move the threshold, or read the ROC curve and AUC, to balance one kind of mistake against the other. Always compare with the majority-class baseline. If you can say these five lines in your own words, you are ready for the lab.

title.text:
Read the workflow before you write it: impute,
standardise, fit, predict probabilities, count

runs.text: imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy=
"median"
X_train = imputer.fit_transform(train_features)
X_valid = imputer.transform(valid_features)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
LogisticRegression())
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_valid)[:, 1]
threshold = 0.5
y_pred = (y_proba >= threshold).astype(int)
cm = confusion_matrix(y_valid, y_pred)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: The imputer fills each missing value (NaN) with the training median (imputation).
The pipeline chains StandardScaler and LogisticRegression.
predict_proba gives a probability per class. Column 1 is the positive class.
y_proba >= threshold gives True or False. astype(int) makes it 1 or 0: y_pred.
confusion_matrix puts Actual down the side and Predicted across the top, negative first: TN and FP in the top row, FN and TP below.

slides.notes:
Before we leave the concepts, look at the workflow. The imputer, SimpleImputer, fills missing values, here with the training median, so a missing value cannot stop the model. X_train is the table of training features, and y_train is the column of labels. Chain StandardScaler and the logistic regression in one pipeline.

Fit it, which learns the means, the standard deviations and the weights from the training set only. Then ask for probabilities, and keep the column for the positive class. Compare each probability with the threshold, here 0.5, to get y_pred, the predicted class. And count the answers in a confusion matrix, cm.

It has the same layout as our slide: Actual down the side, Predicted across the top. If you can read these lines aloud in plain words, you are ready.

title.text:
Four messages you will meet,
what they mean and what to do

rows.text: A missing value (NaN) reached StandardScaler or the model
Run the imputation step (SimpleImputer with the training median)
Classification metrics can't handle a mix of binary and continuous targets
You gave probabilities where a predicted class (0 or 1) was needed
Compare y_proba with the threshold first, to get y_pred
The model stopped before it finished learning. The cell still runs
Standardise the features, or raise max_iter
A cell above has not been run yet
Run all cells from the top, in order

slides.notes:
Messages are normal, and reading them is a skill. Here are the four you will most likely meet today. A NaN error means a missing value reached the model, so run the imputation step. The long message about binary and continuous targets means you gave the metric a probability where it needed a predicted class, so compare the probability with the threshold first.

A convergence warning is only a warning, and it appears when features are not standardised. And a name error means you skipped a cell above. Read the last line of any message first.
